## Proof

The given PDE is the Lagrange linear first-order PDE

$$z(x+y)\,p + z(x-y)\,q = x^{2}+y^{2},\qquad p=\frac{\partial z}{\partial x},\; q=\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}.$$

It has the standard form $Pp+Qq=R$ with

$$P=z(x+y),\quad Q=z(x-y),\quad R=x^{2}+y^{2}.$$

Lagrange's auxiliary (subsidiary) system is

$$\frac{dx}{z(x+y)}=\frac{dy}{z(x-y)}=\frac{dz}{x^{2}+y^{2}}.\tag{1}$$

Two independent first integrals of (1) give the complete integral $\phi(u,v)=0$.

---

### First integral (the given particular solution)

Use the multipliers $(l,m,n)=(x,-y,-z)$.  Check the consistency condition $lP+mQ+nR=0$:

$$x\cdot z(x+y)+(-y)\cdot z(x-y)+(-z)(x^{2}+y^{2})$$
$$=z\bigl[x^{2}+xy-xy+y^{2}\bigr]-z(x^{2}+y^{2})=z(x^{2}+y^{2})-z(x^{2}+y^{2})=0.\;\checkmark$$

Hence, from (1),

$$x\,dx-y\,dy-z\,dz=0\;\Longrightarrow\;d\!\left(\tfrac{x^{2}-y^{2}-z^{2}}{2}\right)=0,$$

so

$$\boxed{x^{2}-y^{2}-z^{2}=u},\tag{2}$$

which is exactly the particular solution supplied in the problem.

---

### Second integral (the required second part)

Use the multipliers $(l,m,n)=(y,x,-z)$.  Verify $lP+mQ+nR=0$:

$$y\cdot z(x+y)+x\cdot z(x-y)+(-z)(x^{2}+y^{2})$$
$$=z\bigl[xy+y^{2}+x^{2}-xy\bigr]-z(x^{2}+y^{2})=z(x^{2}+y^{2})-z(x^{2}+y^{2})=0.\;\checkmark$$

Therefore, from (1),

$$y\,dx+x\,dy-z\,dz=0.$$

Since $y\,dx+x\,dy=d(xy)$ and $z\,dz=d\!\left(\tfrac{z^{2}}{2}\right)$,

$$d(xy)-d\!\left(\tfrac{z^{2}}{2}\right)=0\;\Longrightarrow\;xy-\tfrac{z^{2}}{2}=c_{2}.$$

Multiplying by $2$ and renaming the constant,

$$\boxed{2xy-z^{2}=v}.\tag{3}$$

---

### Verification

From (2): $2x\,dx-2y\,dy-2z\,dz=0$, so $p=\dfrac{x}{z}$ and $q=-\dfrac{y}{z}$.
From (3): $2y\,dx+2x\,dy-2z\,dz=0$, so $p=\dfrac{y}{z}$ and $q=\dfrac{x}{z}$.

For the complete integral $\phi(u,v)=0$ we have, along any solution surface,
$\phi_{u}\,du+\phi_{v}\,dv=0$, i.e.

$$\phi_{u}(2x\,dx-2y\,dy-2z\,dz)+\phi_{v}(2y\,dx+2x\,dy-2z\,dz)=0.$$

Collecting the coefficients of $dx$ and $dy$ and reading off $p=dz/dx$, $q=dz/dy$:

$$p=\frac{x\,\phi_{u}+y\,\phi_{v}}{z(\phi_{u}+\phi_{v})},\qquad q=\frac{-y\,\phi_{u}+x\,\phi_{v}}{z(\phi_{u}+\phi_{v})}.$$

Substituting into the left-hand side of the PDE:

$$z(x+y)p+z(x-y)q=\frac{(x+y)(x\phi_{u}+y\phi_{v})+(x-y)(-y\phi_{u}+x\phi_{v})}{\phi_{u}+\phi_{v}}.$$

The numerator expands to

$$(x+y)(x\phi_{u}+y\phi_{v})+(x-y)(-y\phi_{u}+x\phi_{v})$$
$$=\bigl[x(x+y)-y(x-y)\bigr]\phi_{u}+\bigl[y(x+y)+x(x-y)\bigr]\phi_{v}$$
$$=(x^{2}+y^{2})\phi_{u}+(x^{2}+y^{2})\phi_{v}=(x^{2}+y^{2})(\phi_{u}+\phi_{v}).$$

Hence

$$z(x+y)p+z(x-y)q=\frac{(x^{2}+y^{2})(\phi_{u}+\phi_{v})}{\phi_{u}+\phi_{v}}=x^{2}+y^{2},$$

which is identically the right-hand side of the PDE.  Thus the complete integral

$$\phi\bigl(x^{2}-y^{2}-z^{2},\;2xy-z^{2}\bigr)=0$$

satisfies the PDE for every differentiable $\phi$.

---

### Conclusion

The complete integral of $z(x+y)p+z(x-y)q=x^{2}+y^{2}$ is

$$\phi\bigl(\,x^{2}-y^{2}-z^{2},\;2xy-z^{2}\,\bigr)=0.$$

The first part, $x^{2}-y^{2}-z^{2}=u$, is the particular solution given in the problem. The **second part** of the solution is

$$\boxed{2xy-z^{2}=v}.$$
